newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban offers mutual forces pullback.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban offers mutual forces pullback.

text.p: Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia on Friday offered its opponents a mutual pullback of forces from frontlines north of the capital Kabul as part of a U.N.-proposed ceasefire.

Taleban acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous said the militia would withdraw to its bases in Kabul if its opponents went back to the Panjsher Valley north of the capital and the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Pansher is the stronghold of the ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood and Mazar-i-Sharif is the headquarters of Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Ghous spoke to the Afghan Islamic Press, a Pakistan-based news service on Thursday while in Pakistan for talks with General Paynda, a member of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction representing the northern alliance.
The two were brought together by U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl, who told a news conference the meeting was good but had not produced any immediate result.
The opposition alliance wants demilitarisation of Taleban-held Kabul as a condition for ceasefire.
Ghous said the Taleban forces were not deployed in Kabul but were only defending the capital from positions outside it.
He said the Taleban would never get out of Kabul. "But if they (Masood and Dostum) withdraw their forces to Panjsher and Mazar, we will withdraw ours to bases in Kabul," he said.
He said the Taleban wanted a ceasefire to be enforced by a joint commission of the two sides and it could be monitored by observers from the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Conference.
But he said any deployment of a U.N. peace-keeping force would not be useful.
Previous U.N. efforts to negotiate a ceasefire, which would include arrangements for an exchange of prisioners and bodies, have foundered on differences over what should happen next.
Holl said on Thursday both sides had accepted that there should be a political process likely to focus on demilitarising Kabul and handing the battered city over to a neutral force.
But he said they were still far apart on how far the rival forces should pull back from the capital and what the composition of the neutral security force should be.
He played down one major obstacle to an agreement -- the Taleban's demand that their strict version of Islamic Sharia law should be imposed throughout the country.
Holl said attempting to resolve that issue right away might make it impossible to bring about an urgently needed ceasefire.

Ghous said representatives of Afghan factions, scholars and intellectuals could sit togather to decide about the future of Afghanistan but any system of government must be in accordance with Islamic principles.
